definition: Consensus clustering is a method of aggregating (potentially conflicting) results from multiple clustering algorithms.
details: Also called cluster ensembles or aggregation of clustering (or partitions), it refers to the situation in which a number of different (input) clusterings have been obtained for a particular dataset and it is desired to find a single (consensus) clustering which is a better fit in some sense than the existing clusterings. Consensus clustering is thus the problem of reconciling clustering information about the same data set coming from different sources or from different runs of the same algorithm. When cast as an optimization problem, consensus clustering is known as median partition, and has been shown to be NP-complete, even when the number of input clusterings is three. Consensus clustering for unsupervised learning is analogous to ensemble learning in supervised learning.

explainer.lead: Several clustering methods—or repeated runs of one method—can divide the same dataset in conflicting ways. Consensus clustering reconciles those divisions into a single clustering intended to fit the data better than the individual results.

tiers.eli5: Imagine asking several friends to sort the same collection of toys into groups. They might group them by color, shape, or size, so consensus clustering looks for one grouping that best brings their different answers together.
tiers.practitioner: Collect multiple partitions of the same dataset, whether from different algorithms, different sources, or repeated runs of one algorithm, then optimize a chosen consensus criterion. Treat the optimization cost as a serious constraint: the median-partition formulation is NP-complete even with three input clusterings.
tiers.paperLevel: Given input partitions P1, ..., Pm of one dataset, consensus clustering seeks a single partition P* that reconciles them and is a better fit under some criterion. When formulated as an optimization problem, it is called median partition; this problem is NP-complete even for m = 3. It is the unsupervised-learning analogue of ensemble learning in supervised learning.

explainer.example: Suppose three algorithms each split the same six documents into groups. One puts documents A and B together, another puts B and C together, and the third separates all three; consensus clustering reconciles these conflicting partitions into one final assignment of all six documents.
explainer.intuition: Different clusterings can capture conflicting views of the same data. Consensus clustering looks for a compromise that fits the collection of views better, rather than simply accepting one of them.
howItWorks: Start with one dataset and several clusterings of it.
Obtain those clusterings from different sources, different algorithms, or different runs of the same algorithm.
Compare and reconcile the grouping information in the input clusterings.
Search for one consensus clustering that is a better fit under the chosen criterion.
When this search is cast as optimization, it is called the median-partition problem.
explainer.whyItMatters: It provides a way to combine clustering evidence instead of relying on a single potentially conflicting result. Its value is similar in spirit to ensemble learning in supervised learning, but it applies to unsupervised clustering.
misconceptions: The input clusterings do not have to come from different algorithms; repeated runs of one algorithm also count.
Consensus clustering is not supervised ensemble learning, although the two ideas are analogous.
Finding the optimal consensus is not necessarily easy: median partition is NP-complete even with three inputs.
